case_study_insert.main_stem: Marlowe Activewear (MAW) is a private limited company in the fashion retail sector, selling gym and sports clothing online and employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2014 by Sofia Marlowe, the business operates a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership. MAW plans to invest $640,000 in an automated cutting line and a new e-commerce platform, financed by a $260,000 bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $13 a unit and a selling price of $37, and produces 22,500 units a year. MAW faces a seam defect rate of 4.6% and labour turnover of 11% among its production staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and E-commerce Report — Q4 2025: MAW packed 5,800 orders last quarter, with a seam defect rate of 4.6%, up from 2.9% a year ago. Labour turnover reached 11% and customer complaints about faulty stitching rose to 41 from 23 per month. Average dispatch time was 3.8 days. A survey of 820 online shoppers found 59% would buy more if returns were free and 51% preferred locally made activewear. A skills audit shows 10 of 36 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the regional college costs $660 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marlowe Activewear as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Retail Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of MAW's $260,000 variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.6% from $13.05 to $13.91 an hour from April 2026, raising production payroll costs. (3) Performance-fabric input costs have risen 10.4% year-on-year, while online spending on activewear grew 5.2%.

questions.question_text: MAW is funding its $640,000 expansion with a $260,000 bank loan and $380,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for MAW of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so MAW keeps cash available while installing the $640,000 automated cutting line and e-commerce platform. With a $260,000 bank loan already committed and fixed costs of $270,000 a year, using $380,000 of internal funds avoids extra debt service and leaves more of the $37 selling price to cover the $13 variable cost and absorb the 10.4% rise in performance-fabric input costs.

Point 2: Internal finance imposes no lender covenants or collateral risk, so Sofia Marlowe keeps control of how the new platform is built and where the cutting line is installed. It is quicker than negotiating further borrowing, letting MAW respond to the 4.6% seam defect rate and 11% labour turnover by investing in the new equipment and staff systems immediately rather than waiting for a bank decision. That speed protects the 51% of 820 surveyed shoppers who prefer locally made activewear, since faster, better-quality output supports the brand while the workforce of 36 is stretched by the expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to MAW's expansion financing and operating position.

questions.question_text: MAW wants to raise online sales of its new activewear range. Consider national television advertising, local radio advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MAW choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television could reach a huge audience quickly and build brand awareness for the locally made activewear promoted by 51% of 820 surveyed shoppers. However, airtime is very expensive for a firm with $270,000 fixed costs and a $260,000 bank loan, and many viewers are outside the online customer base, so much of the spend would be wasted given the $640,000 expansion already under way.

Local radio advertising: Radio is cheaper and can target local listeners near the production site with a launch message, supporting the 59% of surveyed shoppers who would buy more with free returns. Its limits are narrow reach for a business that sells online nationally, an audio-only format that cannot show the garments or stitching quality, and little ability to address the 41 complaints about faulty stitching directly.

Social media influencer marketing: Fitness and lifestyle influencers can model the activewear, demonstrate fabric quality and explain the free-returns message to a large, relevant online audience, reaching the 59% who would buy more with free returns and the 51% who prefer locally made products. Engagement can be tracked against the 5,800-order baseline and the 41 stitching complaints. Drawbacks are that reputable influencers charge fees, results accumulate gradually, and a negative comment about the 4.6% defect rate could harm the brand.

Recommendation: MAW should choose social media influencer marketing, with a modest radio reminder in its home region. It displays the product, carries the locally made and free-returns messages, and reaches online shoppers nationwide at far lower cost than television for a $640,000 expansion partly funded by debt. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and radio is rejected as the main channel because it cannot show the clothing or reach the national online market. Sofia Marlowe should monitor the 5,800-order baseline and the 41 complaints before scaling the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to MAW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MAW with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: MAW's labour turnover is 11% and its seam defect rate is 4.6%. Explain two benefits for MAW of using democratic leadership with its workforce of 36.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the workforce of 36, especially sewing and packing staff, to suggest fixes for the 4.6% seam defect rate and the 41 complaints about faulty stitching. Operators who sew the garments daily understand where seams fail, so their ideas are practical, and being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which should reduce the 11% labour turnover that forces repeated hiring and retraining.

Point 2: Involvement gives staff ownership of quality in a hierarchical organisational structure, so the 41 stitching complaints can be addressed through team problem-solving rather than instructions from Sofia Marlowe alone. Higher morale also supports the 51% of 820 surveyed shoppers who prefer locally made activewear: engaged workers check seams carefully, cutting the 4.6% defect rate and the $660-per-employee training cost associated with replacing leavers, while the 22,500-unit output needed for the $640,000 expansion is maintained.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MAW's turnover, defects, structure and output.

questions.question_text: MAW must train 10 of 36 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should MAW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the cutting line and sewing stations is tailored to MAW's own equipment and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 10 trainees productive during the 5,800-order quarter. Supervisors can correct the techniques behind the 4.6% seam defect rate immediately and link training to the 41 stitching complaints. The drawbacks are that experienced operators lose time teaching, bad habits may spread, and no external certificate is awarded.

Off-the-job training: The regional college course at $660 per employee costs 10 × $660 = $6,600, a small sum beside the $640,000 investment. It provides structured, certified sewing and quality skills and removes trainees from production distractions, which matters when defects are rising. However, it takes 10 of a workforce of 36 away from the line during a busy quarter, risking the 3.8-day dispatch target and more than 41 complaints, and generic content may not match MAW's exact machines without follow-up coaching.

Decision: MAW should choose on-the-job training as the main method, adding short certified college modules for senior operators later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids worsening the 41 complaints while democratic leadership already supports peer coaching in the hierarchical structure. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because $6,600 and ten lost shifts would disrupt the 22,500-unit output at a sensitive launch with 11% labour turnover. Sofia Marlowe should pilot coaching with one team, compare the 4.6% defect rate, and only pay the $660 fee where formal certification brings value.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MAW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of MAW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MAW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($37 − $13) = $270,000 ÷ $24 = 11,250 units. Answer: break-even output is 11,250 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $37 − $13 = $24. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MAW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 11,250-unit break-even point with output of 22,500 units gives a margin of safety of 11,250 units, showing how far demand can fall before MAW stops covering its $270,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $24 lets managers model the free-returns offer: funding returns from margin reduces the effective contribution per garment, so they can judge whether the 59% of 820 shoppers who would buy more with free returns generate enough extra orders to compensate.
3. With a $260,000 bank loan to service and $380,000 retained profit committed, the $24 contribution and 22,500-unit output show the cash available for repayments and help phase the $640,000 spending on the cutting line.
4. Unit cost can be checked as $270,000 ÷ 22,500 = $12 plus $13 variable cost = $25 a garment, letting MAW benchmark whether the 4.6% defect rate and 11% labour turnover are pushing costs above target and whether the automated line improves the figure.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 11,250 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 11,250-unit margin of safety against 22,500 output; free-returns decisions using $24 contribution; servicing the $260,000 loan and $640,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $25 against defects and turnover.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MAW's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MAW's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.22 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.84 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.22 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $110,000 inventories + $30,000 trade receivables + $50,000 cash = $190,000; 2025 current assets = $90,000 + $45,000 + $65,000 = $200,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 $190,000 ÷ $95,000 = 2.00 and ($190,000 − $110,000) ÷ $95,000 = $80,000 ÷ $95,000 = 0.84. For 2025, $200,000 ÷ $90,000 = 2.22 and ($200,000 − $90,000) ÷ $90,000 = $110,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.22.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has strengthened on both measures. The first rose from 2.00 to 2.22 because current assets grew from $190,000 to $200,000 while current liabilities fell from $95,000 to $90,000, helped by cash increasing from $50,000 to $65,000. The stock-free measure climbed from 0.84 to 1.22 and is the more significant signal: MAW can now cover its short-term bills from liquid assets alone, without relying on selling the $90,000 of activewear inventory, which is valuable while it services a $260,000 loan and spends $640,000 on the automated cutting line. The reservation is that trade receivables rose from $30,000 to $45,000, tying up cash that could fund the 10.4% fabric-cost increase; if online platform customers or wholesale buyers pay late, the stronger position could erode. Inventories did fall, which is welcome given the 4.6% defect rate.

Conclusion: MAW's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the improvement does not depend on stock, so the business is better able to meet its obligations. Rising receivables are the main risk, so Sofia Marlowe should tighten credit control as the $640,000 expansion proceeds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on the financial position.

questions.question_text: MAW is considering a free-returns policy on its e-commerce platform. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MAW of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Free returns would answer the 59% of 820 surveyed shoppers who said they would buy more if returns were free, removing a barrier to online purchases and supporting the $37 selling price and $24 contribution on each garment. Extra orders would spread the $270,000 fixed costs over more units and help the $640,000 cutting-line investment pay back sooner.

Disadvantage: Handling returns adds reverse-logistics costs and can be abused, reducing the $24 contribution per garment, especially while the seam defect rate is 4.6% and likely to generate avoidable returns. The insert gives no figure for the cost of processing a return or the sales uplift, so the net effect cannot be quantified and the decision must be judged qualitatively. Sofia Marlowe should trial the policy on one product line, compare the 5,800-order baseline and the 41 stitching complaints, and review the 51% who prefer locally made activewear before extending it nationally.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MAW's survey, costs, defects and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.6% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in performance-fabric input costs will affect MAW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If MAW's $260,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $260,000 = $1,950 a year (0.0075 × $260,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $270,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. The rise could make future borrowing dearer and might slightly dampen the 5.2% growth in online activewear spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.6%, to $13.91 an hour): The workforce of 36 includes hourly-paid production and packing staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided, especially with 11% labour turnover. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 22,500 units ÷ 36 staff = 625 garments per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; reducing the 4.6% defect rate and training the 10 untrained staff would help protect it.

Performance-fabric input costs (10.4%): These feed the $13 variable cost on every garment. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $13 were exposed, 10.4% × $13 = $1.352, about $1.35 a garment, and at 22,500 units that is roughly $30,420 a year (22,500 × $1.352). Even a smaller exposed share erodes the $24 contribution on each garment, and the effect repeats on every unit.

Conclusion: The 10.4% rise in performance-fabric input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 22,500 garments and directly attacks the $24 contribution that services the $260,000 loan and funds the $640,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,950 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 625 garments per worker. MAW should cut the 4.6% defect rate and review the $37 price rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MAW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MAW's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
